claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 can be homogenized into a high-temperature, single-phase BCC structure.
Phase stability in the high-temperature BCC state is governed by a balance between a thermodynamic driving force for Cr segregation and kinetic suppression from sluggish diffusion.
High Cr content produces mixing enthalpies that favor phase separation and ordering.
High configurational entropy and reduced atomic mobility delay nucleation and growth of competing phases.
Kinetic suppression stabilizes the BCC structure up to a critical time-temperature threshold.
Isothermal annealing at several elevated temperatures and durations provides a controlled perturbation of transformation kinetics.
An inert atmosphere and controlled cooling rates will minimize extraneous nucleation.
The relevant structural mediators are nanoscale compositional fluctuations and chemical short-range order within the BCC lattice.
The multielement character of the alloy causes significant lattice distortion and sluggish diffusion.
Lattice distortion and sluggish diffusion inhibit diffusion-controlled nucleation and growth of Cr-rich precipitates or other secondary phases.
Transformation begins only when annealing time and temperature are sufficient to overcome kinetic barriers.
At short annealing times or lower temperatures, the BCC phase will remain metastable with minimal compositional modulation.
Increasing annealing duration or temperature beyond a critical threshold will produce Cr segregation and ordered or precipitate phases.

The cited Al-Co-Cr-Fe-Ni aging study reports nanoscale L12 ordered domains after aging at 600 degrees Celsius, supporting thermal-history-dependent ordering in the same elemental alloy system but not Cr segregation in the claimed composition.
Development of segregation, ordering, or precipitates will correlate with a reduction in BCC phase fraction.
Beyond the applicable annealing time-temperature range, the BCC phase will decompose into secondary phases.
The critical transformation temperatures and times are not defined and may depend on minor composition and processing-history variations.
XRD, TEM, and APT measurements before and after annealing can test for phase-fraction changes, nanoscale precipitates, ordering, and Cr segregation relative to the as-homogenized baseline.
Absence of significant Cr enrichment, ordering, precipitation, or phase-composition change across the predicted critical range would falsify the proposed balance mechanism.
